hints.en: like the e in 'bed', held long: Käse, spät — never the 'ay' of 'day' and never English 'a'
say 'ay' as in 'day', then round your lips: Föhn, hören, schön — never 'oh', never 'oy'
say 'ee', then round your lips as if for 'oo' and hold it: üben, Tür, fünf — never English 'oo' and never 'yoo'
sounds like English 'eye': klein = 'kline'. Trick for ei/ie: say the English name of the second letter
long ee as in 'see': Fieber = 'FEE-buh' — the e is silent. Not the same as ei! (In loanwords ending -ie/-ien you do hear it: Familie = 'fa-mee-li-uh'.)
like oy in 'boy': neu = 'noy' — never 'ee-oo'
same oy sound as eu; äu shows the base word had au: Traum → träumen
one sound, English sh as in shoe: Schule = 'shoo-luh' — except before the ending -chen, where it stays s + ch: bisschen, Häuschen

context.en: after e, i, ä, ö, ü, ei, eu/äu and after l, n, r — and always in the ending -chen (Mädchen, Frauchen); never in chs

hints.en: a soft hiss like the h in 'huge': Licht, ich, Milch — never k, never sh

context.en: after a, o, u and au — but never before the diminutive ending -chen, and never in chs

hints.en: a rough throat sound like Scottish 'loch': Nacht, kochen — never plain k

context.en: at the start of a word borrowed from French

hints.en: Chef = 'shef', like sch — not English 'chef' with a ch. (In Greek loans — Chemie, China — northern German uses the soft ich-sound, the south uses k.)
chs inside one stem is a plain 'ks': sechs = 'zeks', wachsen, Fuchs — not the ch sound at all. Where the s belongs to an ending the ch survives: du machst, nächste.

context.en: at the start of a word or syllable before a vowel — but not right after p, k or t (Erbse, Krebse)

hints.en: voiced like English z: Seife = 'ZY-fuh', Sonne = 'ZON-nuh'

context.en: before p or t, at the start of a word or stem — also after prefixes and inside compounds

hints.en: sp- and st- start with sh, also after a prefix: Stift = 'shtift', verstehen = 'fair-SHTAY-en', aufstehen = 'OWF-shtay-en'. Inside a word it stays s: Fenster, kostet.
ss is just s — its job is the vowel in front of it, which is SHORT: essen, Wasser, müssen. ß means that vowel is long: Straße, groß. Every doubled consonant works this way: Sonne, offen.
a sharp s, never a b: groß = 'grohss'; it follows a long vowel or a diphthong — Straße, groß, heißen, weiß
ts as in 'cats', even at the start of a word: Zimmer = 'tsimmer'. tz after a short vowel is the same sound: jetzt, sitzen, putzen — never a buzzing English z.

context.en: at the end of a word or syllable

hints.en: hardens to t at the end: Geld = 'gelt', Freund = 'froynt'

context.en: at the end of a word or syllable

hints.en: hardens to p at the end: Urlaub = 'oor-lowp'

context.en: at the end of a word or syllable

hints.en: hardens to k at the end: Tag = 'tahk'; word-final -ig sounds like -ich (wichtig), but the g comes back before a vowel ending: wichtige

context.en: unstressed at the end of a word

hints.en: final -er is a vowel, not an r: Lehrer = 'LAY-ruh', Fenster = 'FEN-stuh', Wasser = 'VASS-uh' — like the -a in 'sofa'

context.en: after a vowel, when it does not begin a new syllable

hints.en: silent — it only stretches the vowel: Schuh = 'shoo', Stuhl, wohnen = 'VOH-nen'. It is spoken when it starts a syllable, also after a prefix: Uhu, Ahorn, Gehalt, gehabt.
German w is English v: Wasser = 'VASS-uh' — never like English w
usually f: viel = 'feel', Vorsicht, von

context.en: in words borrowed from other languages

hints.en: in loanwords v is a real v: Pullover, Video, Vase
like y in 'yes': Jacke = 'YAH-kuh', ja = 'yah' — only English loanwords (Job, Jeans, joggen) keep the English j
kv, not kw: Quittung = 'KVIT-oong' (oo short, as in 'book')
both letters sound, squeezed into one push: Kopf = 'kopf', Topf, pflanzen — not just f, and not p plus a separate f
